title: the half-golden mongoose
hook: the great sacrifice is finished and praised by all, and a mongoose with half a golden body says it isn't worth a handful of flour
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is God
tomorrow: the Pandavas walk out of the city for the last time. what do they leave behind?

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Ashvamedhika, at Manipura, Arjuna was struck down by his own son, and Ulupi's gem brought him back. Your line was svadharma: do the duty of the role you're in.

Gold handed out to the brahmanas, food for everyone, kings and sages crowding the grounds: the horse is home, the sacrifice is done, and everyone says there's never been a rite like it. Then, from a hole in the ground, out comes a mongoose. One side of its body is gold. It looks around at all this splendor and speaks, in a voice like thunder: this sacrifice of yours isn't equal to a little barley flour given away by a poor brahmana in Kurukshetra. The crowd goes silent.
screen: `THE SACRIFICE IS DONE.` → `A MONGOOSE, HALF GOLD.` → `"NOT EQUAL TO A LITTLE FLOUR."`

segments.voice: In Kurukshetra, the mongoose explains, there lived a brahmana who fed his family by gleaning, picking up the grains left in the fields after harvest. A famine came, and the family went hungry for a long time. At last he gathered enough barley for a little flour, and they divided it four ways: the man, his wife, their son and the son's wife. Just as they were about to eat, a hungry guest arrived. The brahmana welcomed him and gave him his own share. The guest was still hungry. The wife gave hers. Then the son. Then the daughter-in-law. Then the guest revealed himself: he was Dharma, righteousness itself, and the family was carried to heaven. The mongoose had rolled in the scattered flour, and wherever it touched, its fur turned to gold. Half of it. Ever since, it has gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, hoping to turn the other half gold. It just rolled in Yudhishthira's. Nothing changed. Here's the teaching. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells a student going home: let your guest be a god to you, atithi devo bhava. That's why Hindu families feed the guest first, and in this story the guest really was Dharma. And in the Gita, Krishna asks only a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love. A gift is weighed by what it cost and the love in it, not by its size.
screen: `A GLEANER'S FAMILY IN FAMINE` · `FOUR SHARES, ALL GIVEN AWAY` · `THE GUEST WAS DHARMA` · `HALF GOLD, STILL ROLLING` · then, large: `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD`

segments.voice: Rest your hands palms up in your lap, as if holding a small bowl. Many Hindu families set aside the first portion of a meal before anyone eats, for a guest, a cow, or anyone hungry. Think of your last meal, and of who else might have been hungry at that hour. Then think of one small portion, not grand, just real, that you could set aside; if you pray, offer that intention in your prayer, and if you don't, simply decide it.
Ashvamedhika. The book of the horse sacrifice, which ends with a mongoose weighing it against a poor family's flour.
Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. A handful of barley outweighed a king's gold. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The story of the mongoose and the gleaner's flour closes the account of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice in the Ashvamedhika Parva; storytellers retell it to teach that a gift given in want outweighs great display, and that the guest is to be honored as God.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: the mongoose's half-golden body, its thunderous voice, its claim that the sacrifice is not equal to a prastha of barley flour, and the order of giving (brahmana, wife, son, daughter-in-law).
Confirm that the guest was Dharma and that the family went to heaven, and that the mongoose rolled in the flour and the water the guest had used.
The text later identifies the mongoose with Wrath under a curse; this is left out and could be a future day.
Some recensions add a discussion of sacrifice and non-violence after this episode; not covered.
The note that nakula (mongoose) is also the twin's name is a standard lexicon meaning; please confirm wording.
The hook's "there's never been a rite like it" is reported speech of the crowd, not a claim; check it matches the text's praise of the sacrifice.
